case.label: Case study
case.codeblue.title: Code Blue. From UI kit to Design System
case.codeblue.summary: What started as a simple UI kit has evolved into a Design System that supports more than 12 digital products. Beyond component design, it includes a three-level token architecture, governance that works without a dedicated team, and a shared language that has changed how design and development work together at Serviceware.
case.codeblue.meta_team: UX Designers, UX Engineers, Developers, Stakeholders
case.codeblue.h3.gobernanza_distribuida_: Distributed governance with a clear center
case.codeblue.p_001: When I joined Serviceware in 2019, the company managed 5 digital products in production and 3 more under development, built by independent teams, each with its own technology, visual criteria, and level of maturity. There was no design system, so visual and interaction inconsistencies accumulated across products—and often within a single product—creating friction for users and duplicating work in design and development.
case.codeblue.p_002: That is why I started by building a simple UI kit called Code Blue to address the most visible inconsistencies. Over time, more components were added and basic documentation began (version 2.0), but inconsistencies remained across teams because each one used a different technology. This led me to propose and lead a deep update to the current version (3.0): a complete, scalable Design System with a three-level token architecture, component and pattern documentation, real alignment with development, and distributed governance across teams—with me as the decision-making and coherence center.
case.codeblue.p_003: I have been the owner of the Design System from the start, making the main architecture and component design decisions and leading system documentation in collaboration with other designers. I treat Code Blue as an internal product that evolves with its users (design and development teams) rather than as a static library.
case.codeblue.p_004: Before proposing structural changes in Code Blue 3.0, I spent time understanding what was really happening in the products. I conducted a cross-product audit of the main components in use and analyzed how they were designed, evolved, and implemented in each team. This included conversations with Product Designers, Product Owners, Product Leads, and developers across products to understand what helped and what held them back in their day-to-day work with the system.
case.codeblue.p_005: The findings changed my initial approach:
case.codeblue.p_006: The audit made it clear that the problem was not visual—it was structural. Redesigning components was not enough; the foundation they were built on had to be redesigned. That conclusion defined everything that followed.
case.codeblue.p_007: One of the most important technical decisions was redefining the system's token architecture. The challenge was moving from a single layer of primitive tokens to a three-level model that could scale the system without breaking its coherence.
case.codeblue.p_008: This structure made it possible to introduce visual changes (themes, rebranding, density adjustments...) without manually touching multiple components, which had previously been very difficult to manage. It also aligned teams around a single token architecture for the different technologies in use. At this point I was able to convince most teams of the benefits of aligning on implementation, and all but two decided to migrate their development to a common technology (PrimeNG).
case.codeblue.p_009: Each component combines standard patterns with custom pieces designed for specific product cases, such as the Multi-language text input component. All include variants, states, and usage specifications, and function as an agreement between design and development. Components are designed following WCAG 2.1 Level AA accessibility standards. In addition, artificial intelligence plays an increasingly relevant role in my work with the system, as I use it to generate ideas, quick prototypes to test, accelerate component documentation, and run accessibility validations.
case.codeblue.p_010: When it came time to define how the system would be kept alive, the company decided not to create a dedicated Design System team. Responsibility would be distributed across product teams, with a collaborative model.
case.codeblue.p_011: My decision was to take on the role of center and reference: the system needed someone to make final decisions on architecture, components, and patterns, even when contributions came from diverse teams.
case.codeblue.p_013: To keep the system close to real needs, I ran feedback sessions with teams on critical issues such as component and token naming, or what information was truly relevant in documentation to facilitate handoff between design and development.
case.codeblue.p_014: This model has allowed me to balance two needs that seem opposed: system consistency and team autonomy.
case.codeblue.p_015: Code Blue 3.0 supports more than 12 digital products, with 80% adoption among product teams and a 25% reduction in time to implement new components. Most importantly, a shared language has been established between design and development, reducing handoff friction and enabling teams to move forward more efficiently and consistently.
case.codeblue.p_016: Code Blue is a living project, and that forces me to think of it not as something finished but as something in constant evolution. There are four learnings I take from these six years:
case.codeblue.p_017: The system grows at the pace of the product, not the other way around. If I had tried to build Code Blue 3.0 from the start, I would have failed. Starting with a simple UI kit was the right decision—it let us gain traction and build credibility before asking for the investment needed for a full system.
case.codeblue.p_018: A Design System is measured in context, not in isolation. The real challenge is not how good it looks in a component library, but how it behaves when different teams apply it for different purposes.
case.codeblue.p_019: Technical architecture defines the system's ceiling. For years the system worked with primitive tokens and enough discipline, until the lack of a semantic layer began to slow product evolution. The semantic layer is not an implementation detail: it is what separates a library from a living system.
case.codeblue.p_020: Distributed governance works, but it needs a center. A model without a dedicated team can be sustained if someone maintains coherence. I have learned to balance autonomy with a single vision that prevents fragmentation.
case.codeblue.cap.diagrama_de_tokens_en_: Three-level token diagram — Primitives → Semantic → Component
case.agent.title: Agent Workspace. From complex interface to agent-centered tool
case.agent.summary: AI Process Engine is Serviceware's platform that integrates artificial intelligence into enterprise service management. Within it, agents handle customer requests through a ticket system in a central interface: the Agent Workspace. Redesigning this screen started from a structural problem: a poorly prioritized interface put secondary information in the foreground and pushed the agent's critical tools to a second level, directly impacting their efficiency and ability to focus.
case.agent.meta_team: Product Owners, Product Leads, UX Designers, Developers, Stakeholders
case.agent.meta_impact: Ongoing research with more than 10 monthly participants and positive feedback across all redesign iterations
case.agent.h3.research_continuo_como_bas: Continuous research as the foundation for decisions
case.agent.h3.jerarquizar_la_interfaz_la: Prioritizing the interface: conversation at the center
case.agent.p_001: AI Process Engine is Serviceware's IT Service Management platform focused on integrating artificial intelligence into enterprise service management, with the goal of automating processes, reducing manual tasks, and improving the operational efficiency of support teams. Within the platform, agents are primarily responsible for managing customer requests through a ticket system, and their work is concentrated in a single interface: the Agent Workspace.
case.agent.p_002: The existing version of the Workspace had a structural problem: the screen showed too many actions at once without clear hierarchy, making it difficult for the agent to quickly identify what information was relevant at any given moment. Key features such as the conversation with the user or access to ticket history competed for visibility with less relevant elements, creating high cognitive load in an environment where workload volume is high and time pressure is constant.
case.agent.p_003: The challenge was not only visual but structural, because the interface was not aligned with the real tasks agents needed to perform. That raised a concrete question: how do you reorganize a complex screen so the agent can focus on what really matters?
case.agent.p_004: As Product Designer on the AI Process Engine project, I led the redesign of the Agent Workspace in collaboration with other UX Designers, Product Owners, Product Leads, and the development team. My responsibility covered the research process, design strategy definition, interface hierarchy reorganization, and functional improvements aimed at optimizing agents' workflow.
case.agent.p_005: Before proposing any structural changes, it was necessary to understand how agents actually worked. I carried out a continuous research process based on interviews with agents, consultants, and stakeholders, combined with monthly tests with more than ten participants throughout the project. During these sessions we analyzed real workflows, the most frequent tasks, friction points, and the strategies users used to find information.
case.agent.p_006: The insights were concrete: the conversation with the customer was the central tool of the agent's work and had to hold a priority place in the interface; agents needed quick access to specific information within the system; and flexibility to adapt the screen to different workflows was a real need, not optional.
case.agent.p_007: Based on research insights, the first decision was to completely reorganize the interface hierarchy. The customer conversation panel, which until then competed for visibility with less relevant elements, became the central, priority element of the screen, allowing the agent to follow incident context clearly and continuously.
case.agent.p_008: Along with this structural change, I incorporated functional improvements aimed at facilitating access to information: search within message history and filters to quickly locate relevant content within the conversation.
case.agent.p_009: Research showed that agents did not all work the same way, so the interface needed to adapt to different working styles without adding complexity. I designed the ability to show or hide panels according to each agent's needs at any given moment, allowing each user to configure their workspace flexibly without leaving the main screen.
case.agent.p_010: This decision also included applying the new Design System (Code Blue 3.0): new components, token architecture, and WCAG accessibility standards, making Agent Workspace one of the first products to adopt the new version of the system in a high information-density context.
case.agent.p_011: The Agent Workspace redesign transformed a complex, poorly prioritized interface into a tool centered on agents' real tasks. With conversation as the main element of the screen, agents can follow the context of each incident clearly and continuously, without moving between different places to find the information they need.
case.agent.p_012: The continuous validation process, with monthly tests throughout the project, made it possible to iterate design decisions on solid ground and detect in time aspects that did not work as expected. Feedback from agents, consultants, and stakeholders who participated in the sessions was positive across all iterations, especially valuing the clarity of the new hierarchy and the flexibility to adapt the interface to different workflows.
case.agent.p_013: The Agent Workspace redesign left me with two learnings I now apply to any redesign project in complex operational environments.
case.agent.p_014: What users ask for is not always what they need. During research, many agents expressed concrete preferences about specific features. However, when we analyzed those preferences within real workflows in tests, priorities changed. This reinforced the importance of continuously validating design decisions with prototypes and in-context tests, rather than making decisions solely from what users state in interviews.
case.agent.p_015: In high information-density environments, simplifying is a structural decision, not a visual one. The previous version of the Workspace did not have an aesthetic problem—it had a hierarchy problem. Reducing the agent's cognitive load was not about removing visual elements, but about reorganizing what information took center stage and what stayed at a second level.
case.portal.title: Portal Page Configuration. From designing pages to configuring content
case.portal.summary: During the migration of the Portal to version 3.0, I worked on redesigning the page configuration process for the administrator role. What initially seemed like a grid usability problem turned out to reveal a deeper issue: the system forced users to build layouts manually when they actually only needed to configure content for a specific goal.
case.portal.meta_impact: Reduced friction through guided responsive templates
case.portal.h3.cambiar_el_modelo_mental_: Changing the mental model: from building to configuring
case.portal.h3.centralizar_la_configurac: Centralizing configuration in a single panel
case.portal.p_001: Serviceware Portal is the platform that acts as a unified access point to the different applications in the Serviceware product ecosystem. Its widget-based architecture allows organizations to customize the portal according to their needs, adapting it to different roles, contexts, and devices. Users with the administrator role are responsible for creating the different screens of the tool and managing their content through widgets.
case.portal.p_002: During the migration from Portal 2.5 to Portal 3.0—a complete redesign adopting the new version of the Design System (Code Blue 3.0) and new technology (PrimeNG)—an in-depth analysis of the page configuration flow revealed a more structural problem than it initially appeared. Widget distribution was based on a cell grid where each widget always started from a generic size (2 columns × 1 row), forcing the administrator to resize it manually as the first step every time they added a new one. In addition, the full flow had to be repeated for the mobile version.
case.portal.p_003: The most relevant insight came from research: most administrators configured pages with one or two widgets at most. The question was no longer how to simplify the grid, but whether it still made sense to ask the administrator to design pages when what they needed was to configure content.
case.portal.p_004: I have been the Product Designer on the Portal team since the project started in 2019. On this project I led the complete redesign of the page configuration flow, from initial discovery and conceptual definition through final design delivery and support during implementation.
case.portal.p_005: Reframing the problem was the first step. The grid assumed the administrator acted as a page builder, making constant decisions about position, size, and widget distribution. But the reality was that administrators did not want to design pages—they wanted to configure content to achieve concrete goals.
case.portal.p_006: The decision was to change that process: instead of asking the administrator to build the page from scratch, I proposed a system based on preconfigured layouts that only needed to be filled with widgets, eliminating the need to configure the layout twice for desktop and mobile.
case.portal.p_007: To decide which layouts should be part of the system, I ran a discovery process combining sessions with internal consultants, stakeholders (Product Owners, Customer Success, and business), and benchmarking of similar products. The result was an initial set of 12 predefined responsive templates.
case.portal.p_008: To reduce fragmentation, I decided to centralize all configuration in a single side panel structured in three tabs: General, Appearance, and Widgets.
case.portal.p_009: The redesign transformed the administrator's way of working, moving from a system oriented toward building pages from scratch to choosing a layout and focusing on configuring content. Stakeholder feedback was especially positive, highlighting reduced friction and a greater sense of control despite having reduced flexibility.
case.portal.p_010: The real problem does not always match the initial request. The need seemed to center on simplifying the grid, but the problem was in the mental model we imposed on the administrator.
case.portal.p_011: More flexibility does not always mean a better experience. Reducing decisions through predefined templates allowed administrators to complete configuration with more clarity and a sense of control.
case.portal.p_012: In B2B environments, operational knowledge is also research. Triangulating knowledge from internal consultants, stakeholders, and usage analysis let me make well-founded decisions without a formal recurring user research process.
case.portal.cap.panel_lateral_general_ap: Side panel — General, Appearance, and Widgets
case.ai.title: AI Solution Assistant. Designing the conversational experience for agents
case.ai.summary: AI Process Engine is Serviceware's platform that integrates artificial intelligence into enterprise service management. Within it, I designed a conversational assistant that supports agents in their daily work. My work covered the default view, message types, ways to integrate the panel on screen, and interaction patterns that make AI useful without interrupting the agent's workflow.
case.ai.meta_team: Product Owners, Product Leads, UX Designers, Developers, Stakeholders, AI Specialists
case.ai.meta_impact: Design adopted as reference for assistant integration in other ecosystem projects
case.ai.h3.la_vista_por_defecto_utilidad: The default view: utility from the first moment
case.ai.h3.el_dise_o_de_los_mensajes_cla: Message design: clarity and action in every response
case.ai.h3.la_integraci_n_del_panel_en_l: Panel integration on screen: adapting to the agent's flow
case.ai.p_001: AI Process Engine is Serviceware's IT Service Management platform focused on integrating artificial intelligence into enterprise service management, with the goal of automating processes, reducing manual tasks, and improving the operational efficiency of support teams. Within the platform, agents are the primary users, responsible for managing customer requests through a ticket system in the Agent Workspace.
case.ai.p_002: In that context, the need arose to create a conversational assistant to accompany the agent during their work. The challenge was not only to design a chat, but to define how an AI assistant should appear within a high information-density operational tool, where the agent's focus is on resolving tickets—not on learning to interact with a new interface.
case.ai.p_003: As Product Designer on the AI Process Engine project, I led the visual design of the AI Solution Assistant experience, working closely with the product, development, and AI specialist teams. My responsibility covered the visual definition of the assistant: the default view and its quick-access options, the design of message types and their interaction patterns, the different ways to integrate the panel on screen, and the assistant's proactive behaviors when it detects situations relevant to the agent.
case.ai.p_004: When the assistant has no conversation history, a blank screen adds nothing for the agent. I designed a default view that shows quick actions oriented to the role's most frequent tasks, so the assistant is useful from the first moment without needing to learn how to interact with it. I also defined proactive behavior for cases where the system automatically detects a problem with the active ticket when landing on the screen, showing an alert message without the agent having to ask.
case.ai.p_005: The conversation between the agent and the assistant needed a message system that was clear, useful, and actionable. I designed the different message types that structure the conversation: the ability to see the information source each response is based on, rating options through like and dislike, action buttons when the response requires action from the agent with the most common option visually highlighted, and transition states such as the indicator that the assistant is generating a response.
case.ai.p_006: An assistant that imposes itself over existing content or is hard to manage quickly becomes an obstacle. I designed two integration modes for different usage profiles: a floating view for agents who consult the assistant occasionally, and an integrated view on screen for those who keep it always visible as part of their usual flow.
case.ai.p_007: The AI Solution Assistant design established the foundations of the conversational experience within the Agent Workspace. Agents now have an assistant that supports their work without interrupting their flow, with a default view oriented to their most frequent tasks, clear and actionable messages, and a panel that adapts to how they work.
case.ai.p_008: Feedback from stakeholders and AI specialists who participated in the review was positive, especially valuing the visual clarity of messages and the coherence of the experience with the rest of the product. The design was also adopted as a reference for integrating the assistant in other ecosystem projects, validating that the decisions made can scale beyond the initial use case.
case.ai.p_009: Designing the AI Solution Assistant left me with two learnings I now apply to any project where AI is part of the experience.
case.ai.p_010: Designing for AI means designing for uncertainty. A conversational assistant does not always give perfect answers, and design must account for that reality. Including the information source, response rating options, or the indicator that the assistant is generating a response are not aesthetic details—they are mechanisms that help the agent evaluate the reliability of what they see and maintain control over the conversation.
case.ai.p_011: A useful tool is one that does not interrupt. On a high information-density screen like the Agent Workspace, the greatest risk of a new assistant is not that it is not useful, but that it competes with the work the agent is already doing. Integration decisions (floating vs integrated view, quick actions in the default view, proactive behavior) do not respond to aesthetic preferences, but to a concrete question: how does the assistant do its job without getting in the way of the agent's?
case.ai.cap.vista_por_defecto: Default assistant view with quick actions
case.ai.cap.tipos_de_mensajes: Composition of the different message types
case.parking.title: Parking Spot. Eliminating an everyday office problem
case.parking.summary: At one of Serviceware's offices, parking is shared and not all employees have a permanently assigned spot, which created friction and conflict in daily management. When a colleague identified the problem and proposed designing a solution, I got involved to shape the experience, becoming the designer on the project and working closely with him from ideation through to the final result.
case.parking.meta_impact: 100% adoption among employees (+30 people) with no incidents since July 2025
case.parking.h3.definir_el_alcance_del_m: Defining MVP scope: what to solve first
case.parking.h3.dos_perfiles_con_flujos_: Two profiles with clear flows and distinct responsibilities
case.parking.h3.prototipar_r_pido_y_vali: Rapid prototyping and validation with users at hand
case.parking.p_001: At one of Serviceware's offices, building parking is shared with other companies, so not all employees have a permanently assigned spot. The situation created an everyday problem: some employees had spots they did not use on certain days while others needed to park without visibility into which spots were available, leading to friction and conflict between colleagues.
case.parking.p_002: The solution came from a colleague's initiative who, upon identifying the problem, proposed designing a mobile application so employees could view available spots and manage assignment transparently, eliminating the informal management that existed until then. The challenge was to design a daily-use tool that any employee could use in a few seconds, without friction and without prior learning.
case.parking.p_003: I got involved in the project voluntarily, taking on the designer role from the ideation phase. My work covered defining features and user flows, the application's information architecture, visual design of screens and their states, rapid prototyping, and testing with colleagues whose feedback helped refine the solution before moving to development.
case.parking.p_004: The first decision was determining which features the MVP should include and which could wait for future iterations. Before defining anything, I analyzed existing shared-resource management applications to identify useful interaction patterns and capture ideas that could apply to the office context. That analysis, combined with direct knowledge of the problem we already had, let us focus quickly on the most frequent scenarios without starting from scratch.
case.parking.p_005: Working with my colleague, we defined the essential features: the ability to release an assigned spot when the employee was not going to the office, and to reserve an available spot with automatic assignment to the first employee who requested it. We also added an alert system so employees without a spot could receive a notification when one was released, without having to monitor the application constantly.
case.parking.p_006: Based on the defined features, we structured the application around two profiles with distinct needs and flows. The employee profile covered everyday actions: checking whether they had an assigned spot, releasing it, reserving an available one, and managing alerts. The administrator profile covered system management: onboarding new employees, assigning fixed parking days, and registering new spots the company could acquire.
case.parking.p_007: The priority in both profiles was the same: each action should be resolvable in few steps and without ambiguity, so the application required no prior learning.
case.parking.p_008: For visual design I used the early versions of Code Blue as a base, which in addition to ensuring coherence and quality in components, helped identify improvement opportunities in the system itself that were incorporated in later versions.
case.parking.p_009: As an internal tool with direct access to end users, I could validate design decisions continuously and without friction. I designed rapid prototypes to validate interactions, comprehension, and copy, and tested them directly with office colleagues. Their feedback allowed us to adjust screens and flows before development, significantly shortening iteration cycles.
case.parking.p_010: This proximity to users was one of the most distinctive aspects of the project compared to typical B2B environments, where direct access to end users is much more limited.
case.parking.p_011: Parking Spot became a functional MVP that directly and effectively resolved friction in office parking management. Since its rollout in July 2025, 100% of office employees use the application, validating that the solution was simple and clear enough to be adopted without friction or prior training.
case.parking.p_012: The most concrete impact is that no conflict related to parking management has occurred since. What was previously resolved informally and created tension between colleagues now happens transparently and automatically through the application.
case.parking.p_013: The project left me with two learnings I now apply especially in small-scale projects and internal tools.
case.parking.p_014: A well-defined MVP is more valuable than a perfect solution. The temptation in any project is to want to solve everything from the start. In Parking Spot, the decision to focus on the three most frequent scenarios—releasing a spot, reserving an available spot, and managing alerts—made it possible to have a functional, adopted solution in record time. Solving the essentials well was more effective than trying to cover every possible case from the beginning.
case.parking.p_015: Direct access to end users changes the pace of design. In most B2B projects, access to end users is limited and requires planning. In Parking Spot the users were my own office colleagues, which allowed continuous, informal validation of decisions, real-time adjustment of screens and flows, and arriving at development with an already validated solution. That proximity is a privilege not always available—and when it is, it is worth making the most of it.
case.melia.title: Meliá Rewards. Redesigning a loyalty program experience
case.melia.summary: Meliá Rewards is Meliá Hotels International's loyalty program, designed to encourage customer repeat visits through point accumulation and exclusive benefits. Its website redesign started from a structural problem: users did not understand the program's real value, navigation created friction when accessing benefits, and the experience was not aligned with the hotel booking process.
case.melia.meta_team: Product Team, Developers, Visual Designer, Stakeholders
case.melia.meta_impact: NPS above 85% and very positive scores in usability tests
case.melia.h3.research_exhaustivo_como_b: Thorough research as the foundation for decisions
case.melia.h3.redefinir_la_arquitectura_: Redefining information architecture from the user's mental model
case.melia.h3.simplificar_la_navegaci_n_: Simplifying navigation, prototyping, and validating with users
case.melia.p_001: Meliá Rewards is Meliá Hotels International's loyalty program that lets customers earn points for stays and access exclusive benefits such as room upgrades, late check-out, or premium services. The program had its own website where users could manage their profile, check their points, and access their benefits, but the experience had structural problems that directly affected perception of the program's value.
case.melia.p_002: The information architecture made it difficult for users to understand how the program worked and what benefits they received at their level. Information about points, advantages, and user status was fragmented across different sections, requiring multiple steps to access basic actions. In addition, the program experience was not aligned with users' real expectations or business objectives, as the hotel booking process, information organization, and navigation flows worked in disconnected ways.
case.melia.p_003: As UX Designer on the project, I led the user research process and defined the information architecture and navigation flows for the redesign. I worked closely with the product team in Meliá Rewards' loyalty department to ensure design decisions aligned with the program's strategic objectives and business vision. I also collaborated with a Visual Designer who handled the final aesthetic layer, while my functional prototypes included their own visual layer to validate interactions and flows with real users before moving to final design.
case.melia.p_004: Before proposing any structural changes, it was necessary to deeply understand how users interacted with the program and where the greatest friction points were. The research process combined different qualitative and quantitative techniques: a heuristic analysis of the product to identify usability problems and inconsistencies, interviews with real program users to understand their expectations and behaviors, usability tests to detect problems, and focus group sessions to deepen understanding of perceived program value.
case.melia.p_005: The insights were concrete: users did not clearly understand how the program worked or how to progress between levels, managing points and benefits required too many steps within navigation, and there was a clear disconnect between the loyalty program and the hotel booking process that affected perceived coherence of Meliá's digital ecosystem.
case.melia.p_006: With research insights defined, the most important decision was to completely redefine the program's information architecture. To validate that the new structure aligned with users' mental models, we used card sorting, a technique that reveals how users naturally organize and group information.
case.melia.p_007: Based on the results, we reorganized content prioritizing what mattered most to the user at each moment: their level within the program, available benefits, and the most relevant actions. The goal was for any user to immediately understand their situation within the program and associated advantages, without navigating multiple sections for basic information.
case.melia.p_008: With the architecture defined, the next decision was to simplify navigation flows to facilitate access to the most frequent actions from any device. This also included aligning the program experience with the hotel booking process, resolving the disconnect users had identified in research.
case.melia.p_009: Design was developed iteratively through functional prototypes in Axure and Sketch, to which I added my own visual layer so validation sessions with users were as realistic as possible. Each iteration was tested with real users, making it possible to adjust flows, visual hierarchy, and copy before final design, reducing the risk of implementation errors.
case.melia.p_010: The Meliá Rewards redesign had a direct, measurable impact on user experience. Usability tests with real program users yielded an NPS above 85% and very positive SUS scores, validating that the design decisions adopted aligned with users' real expectations.
case.melia.p_011: Beyond metrics, the project made it possible to define a prioritized roadmap of future improvements from insights gathered during research, connecting design decisions directly to the loyalty program's strategic objectives.
case.melia.p_012: The project left me with two learnings I now apply to any project where experience has a relevant strategic and business component.
case.melia.p_013: Information architecture is the foundation of any understandable experience. In Meliá Rewards the problem was not visual—it was structural. Users did not understand the program's value because information was organized following internal business logic, not users' mental models. Using card sorting to validate how users themselves organized information was the decision that made it possible to build an architecture that truly worked for them.
case.melia.p_014: Validating with real users changes design decisions. During research, many of our initial hypotheses about the program's problems turned out to be incorrect or incomplete. Interviews, usability tests, and focus groups revealed friction that was not visible from inside the project. That gap between what the team assumed and what users actually experienced reinforced for me the importance of researching before designing, even when the problem seems obvious.
case.codeblue.li_001: Several components were duplicated or implemented inconsistently across products.
case.codeblue.li_002: Existing tokens were at the primitive level, without a semantic layer to abstract their meaning within the interface.
case.codeblue.li_003: Some components were built for very specific use cases and could not scale to other contexts.
case.codeblue.li_004: Primitive tokens: the system's base values (color palette, type scales, spacing).
case.codeblue.li_005: Semantic tokens: a layer that describes a token's intent in the interface (background, text, border, icon), decoupling visual values from their use.
case.codeblue.li_006: Component tokens: the layer that connects the token architecture to concrete implementations, allowing each component to adapt without affecting the global system.
case.codeblue.li_007: Define a clear contribution process: any team need goes through a systemic audit before becoming a new component or variant.
case.codeblue.li_008: Act as the system's design QA, ensuring every change maintains visual and functional consistency.
case.codeblue.li_009: Centralize documentation and principles in a combined Figma, Storybook, and ZeroHeight ecosystem accessible to all teams.
case.codeblue.li_010: Establish adaptation periods for changes that affect multiple products, avoiding blocking development.
